items.stem: The novel that most fully endorsed 1920s business philosophy was

option_explanations.A: Main Street (1920) satirized small-town life and its boosterism — Sinclair Lewis mocked the business mentality, he did not endorse it.
option_explanations.B: The Great Gatsby (1925) critiqued the hollowness of Jazz Age wealth — Fitzgerald exposed the emptiness behind the glitter, not a celebration of business philosophy.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Bruce Barton's The Man Nobody Knows (1925) recast Jesus as a master salesman and businessman — a direct celebration of commerce and advertising, the decade's definitive endorsement of business philosophy.
option_explanations.D: Babbitt (1922) satirized the conformist businessman — Lewis held George Babbitt up for ridicule, not admiration.

items.explanation: Hoover's landslide showed faith in Republican prosperity, the salience of Prohibition, and anti-Catholic resistance to Al Smith — but it did not heal the urban-rural divide, which yawned wider than ever.
options: A. Voters credited Republicans for prosperity
C. Prohibition remained a hot-button issue
D. America rejected a Catholic candidate
items.stem: Hoover's 1928 election demonstrated all of the following EXCEPT

option_explanations.A: Voters really did credit Republicans for prosperity in 1928 — 'a chicken in every pot' Hoover ran on continued Republican good times. This was demonstrated by the election, not the exception.
option_explanations.B: Correct — this is the exception. The urban-rural divide did not fade in 1928 — it yawned wider than ever, with Smith carrying the big cities and Hoover sweeping the countryside. The election exposed the split, it did not heal it.
option_explanations.C: Prohibition really did remain a hot-button issue in 1928 — Smith was wet, Hoover dry, and the issue divided voters sharply. This was demonstrated, not the exception.
option_explanations.D: America really did reject a Catholic candidate in 1928 — anti-Catholic prejudice hurt Al Smith badly, especially in the South and Midwest. This was demonstrated, not the exception.

items.explanation: The 'Lost Generation' -- Hemingway, Fitzgerald, Dos Passos -- fled to Paris, where Gertrude Stein's salon became their headquarters. Exile was itself the critique: they found the prosperous America Parker satirized spiritually empty and went abroad to write about it.
options: A. they joined the Communist Party in large numbers
B. they abandoned literature for electoral politics
C. they moved to Paris and wrote as expatriates
D. they emigrated to the Soviet Union
items.stem: Many American writers of the 1920s, disillusioned with American life, responded by
items.stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

Reviewing Aimee Semple McPherson's autobiography, Dorothy Parker archly treats the celebrity evangelist's book as show business — entertaining, sensational, and revealing how thoroughly religion, like everything else in the 1920s, had become a form of mass entertainment.
—After Dorothy Parker's review of McPherson's This Is That, 1920s

option_explanations.A: American writers did not join the Communist Party in large numbers in the 1920s. The characteristic response of the disillusioned was exile, not party membership.
option_explanations.B: They did not abandon literature for electoral politics — they kept writing. Their response was to write from abroad, not to run for office.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The 'Lost Generation' — Hemingway, Fitzgerald, Dos Passos — moved to Paris, where Gertrude Stein's salon became their headquarters. Exile was itself the critique: they found prosperous America spiritually empty and went abroad to write about it.
option_explanations.D: They did not emigrate to the Soviet Union — their chosen exile was Paris, not Moscow. The Lost Generation's destination was literary Paris.
